content:
We have carbon NMR data: list of chemical shifts. Need number of methyl (CH3) groups. Methyl carbons typically appear around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, maybe 20-30. In data we have peaks: 168.30 (likely carbonyl), 130.70,130.27,128.35,126.66,124.85,123.57 (aromatic), 58.70 (maybe O-CH3 or CH2 attached to hetero), 36.40 (twice), 26.40.

Methyl carbon likely at 26.40 (maybe CH3 attached to something). Also 36.40 could be CH2 or CH3 attached to aromatic? But typical methyl attached to aromatic (toluene) appears ~21 ppm. 36 ppm is more like CH attached to hetero or CH2. 58.70 is likely O-CH3 (methoxy) carbon (CH3 attached to O) appears ~55 ppm. So that is a methyl group as well (O-CH3). So we have at least two methyl groups: one OCH3 (58.70) and one aliphatic CH3 (26.40). The 36.40 peaks could be CH2 (maybe CH2 groups). Since they appear twice, could be two equivalent CH2 groups. Not methyl.

Thus answer likely 2.

But need to be sure: Could there be more methyls hidden? The carbon NMR only shows distinct carbon environments. If there were two equivalent methyl groups they'd appear as one peak. Could be more than one methyl of same environment. But we cannot know. The question likely expects counting distinct methyl groups based on NMR peaks. Usually they'd ask "How many methyl groups are present?" meaning count of CH3 groups in molecule, not distinct signals. Could be deduced from integration of 1H NMR, but we only have carbon. However we can also get 1H NMR to see integration. Let's get proton NMR.
